To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people are not as likely to help a victim of terrorism as they are a victim of other crimes, (2) people are more likely to help a terrorist victim when the terrorist is a foreigner, (3) people are more motivated to help victims when the victim is a woman,

the more a person identifies with a group, and the more that group is perceived as being in a state of conflict with another group, the more likely that person is to be aggressive toward members of that other group.

(a) the more people perceive a threat from terrorism, the more they support aggressive counterterrorist policies, (b) the more people support aggressive counterterroristic policies, the more they perceive that these policies are likely to increase the threat from terrorism, and (c) the more people think that aggressive counterterrorist polices will increase the threat from terrorist attacks, the more they will oppose these policies.
